newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Amnesty mulled for almost half Russia's prisoners.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty mulled for almost half Russia's prisoners.

text.p: Alarmed at conditions in Russia's cramped and overcrowded jails, the prosecutor general said on Wednesday he was drawing up a project to amnesty nearly half the country's one million prisoners.
"We have a project for an amnesty which I will present in a meeting with the president (Boris Yeltsin)," Prosecutor General Yuri Skuratov told a news conference at Interfax news agency.
He said that if the proposal was passed by parliament, the number amnestied "would amount to around 440,000 prisoners". He gave no further details.
Skuratov has warned of a "social explosion" if measures are not taken to improve conditions in Russia's overcrowded prisons.
The flood of crime which has engulfed Russia since the end of the Soviet Union in 1991 has left the country's penal system unable to cope. Almost one in every 100 adult Russians is now behind bars.
Of Russia's million-strong prison population, about 280,000 inmates are awaiting trial.

A report published by human rights group Amnesty International in April cited one case of overcrowding in Moscow's Matrosskaya Tishina prison where 140 prisoners were crowded into a room 70 metres square designed for 35 inmates.

However, the release of hundreds of thousands of prisoners is sure to alarm ordinary Russians, fed up with the dramatic decline in law and order and who retain a strong nostalgia for the virtually crime-free streets of Soviet times.
On Tuesday, Russia's interior minister said crime had eased in the first four months of this year, with registered cases down 10 percent over the same period in 1996.
Skuratov also defended the authorities' record, saying people had been charged for 81 percent of the murders in the first four months of this year, up from 73.5 percent in 1996.

But a list of contract killings of well-known public figures remain unsolved and Skuratov said his organisation's fight against corruption was dogged like so many other Russian institutions by a lack of cash.

"The salary of those working in the prosecutor general's office is now much less than an ordinary bureaucrat's and they have to deal with dead bodies and risk their lives," Skuratov said. "People are just leaving the service," he said.
